title: Andrew Jackson
description: President of the United States from 1829 to 1837
wiki_lead:
Andrew Jackson (March 15, 1767 – June 8, 1845) was the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837. He rose to fame as a U.S. Army general and served in both houses of the U.S. Congress. His political philosophy, which dominated his presidency, became the basis for the rise of Jacksonian democracy. His legacy is controversial: being praised as an advocate for white working Americans and preserving the union of states, and criticized for his racist policies, particularly towards Native Americans.
Born in the colonial Carolinas before the American Revolutionary War, Jackson became a frontier lawyer, married Rachel Donelson, and briefly represented Tennessee in both the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate. After resigning, he served as a Tennessee Superior Court justice from 1798 to 1804. He founded The Hermitage and became a wealthy planter who profited from the forced labor of hundreds of enslaved African Americans. As commander of the Tennessee militia, he led troops in the Creek War of 1813–1814, winning the Battle of Horseshoe Bend and negotiating the Treaty of Fort Jackson, which forced the indigenous Creek to cede vast tracts of the present day states of Alabama and Georgia. In the concurrent war against the British, Jackson's victory at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. He later commanded United States forces during the First Seminole War; his campaign was one of the factors that prompted Spain to negotiate the cession of Florida to the United States.
Jackson briefly served as Florida's first territorial governor before returning to the Senate. He ran for president in 1824, winning a plurality of the popular and electoral vote. Because no candidate secured the electoral majority, the House of Representatives elected John Quincy Adams with the support of Henry Clay, who later joined Adams's cabinet. Jackson's supporters, who alleged that Adams and Clay had formed a "corrupt bargain", created a new political coalition that would become the Democratic Party.
Jackson ran again in 1828, defeating Adams in a landslide victory despite issues such as his slave trading and "irregular" marriage. In 1830, he signed the Indian Removal Act. This act, which has been described as ethnic cleansing, displaced tens of thousands of Native Americans from their ancestral homelands east of the Mississippi River. It resulted in thousands of deaths in what has become known as the Trail of Tears. Jackson faced a challenge to the integrity of the federal union when South Carolina threatened to nullify a high protective tariff set by the federal government. He threatened the use of military force to enforce the tariff, but the crisis was defused when it was amended. In 1832, he vetoed a bill by Congress to reauthorize the Second Bank of the United States, viewing the Bank as a branch of government run by the elite. After a lengthy struggle, the Bank was dismantled. In 1835, Jackson became the only U.S. president to pay off the national debt. After leaving office, he supported the presidencies of Martin Van Buren and James K. Polk, as well as the annexation of Texas.
Opinions about Jackson are often polarized. Supporters characterize him as a defender of democracy and the U.S. Constitution, while critics point to his reputation as a demagogue who ignored the law when it suited him. Scholarly rankings of U.S. presidents historically placed Jackson high in the ranking of presidents. In recent decades, his reputation has declined and his ranking has fallen.

Early life


Childhood
Andrew Jackson was born on March 15, 1767, in the Waxhaws region of the Carolinas. His parents, Andrew Jackson and Elizabeth Hutchinson, were Scots-Irish Presbyterians, whose ancestors had crossed into northern Ireland from Scotland after the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. They emigrated from Ulster, Ireland, in 1765. Jackson had two older brothers who came with his parents from Ireland, Hugh (born 1763) and Robert (born 1764).
grok_lead: Andrew Jackson (March 15, 1767 â June 8, 1845) was an American lawyer, planter, general, and statesman who served as the seventh president of the United States from 1829 to 1837. Born to Scotch-Irish immigrant parents in the Waxhaws region along the border of North and South Carolina, Jackson was orphaned at age 14 after his family perished during the American Revolutionary War, in which he briefly served as a courier and endured capture by British forces. He self-educated in law, moved to Tennessee, built a successful plantation at The Hermitage, and entered politics as a state legislator, judge, and U.S. congressman before rising to military prominence. Jackson's military career included decisive victories in the Creek War of 1813â1814, where he crushed the Red Stick faction at Horseshoe Bend, and the Battle of New Orleans in 1815, repelling a British invasion force despite being outnumbered, which elevated him to national hero status despite the war's prior end by treaty. His campaigns extended to the First Seminole War, securing Florida from Spanish control through unauthorized incursions that pressured U.S. acquisition of the territory. As president, Jackson championed policies favoring agrarian interests and expanded executive authority, vetoing the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States in 1832 on grounds of its unconstitutionality and favoritism toward elites, vetoing more bills than all prior presidents combined, and paying off the national debt in 1835âthe only time in U.S. history. He signed the Indian Removal Act of 1830, authorizing negotiated or coerced treaties to relocate southeastern Native American tribes west of the Mississippi River to facilitate white settlement, a policy that resulted in the Trail of Tears, during which thousands of Cherokee and other tribes perished from disease, exposure, and violence amid forced marches. Known for his combative temperament, involvement in duels, and defense of personal honorâincluding killing a rival in 1806âJackson embodied frontier individualism and populism, founding the Democratic Party and mobilizing common voters against entrenched interests, though his tenure also featured the Nullification Crisis, where he threatened force against South Carolina's resistance to federal tariffs.
